account:
Today has been busy, but several pieces of town business remain unclear to me. I made the scheduled mill inspection and have kept my appointments, including tea with my neighbour. I am now leaving to return to the office for half past four. The authorized great hall lighting inspection with builder is at eighteen; my neighbour says the lighting looks splendid and builder intends to escort me.

The bread business seems unusually active. The secretary's report records freight arranging an order of two hundred loaves with the baker: twenty-four emeralds and seventy-two wheat had been received, with another five hundred twenty-eight wheat needed at that time. Today the secretary observed seventy-three hay bales at the mill stall, but neither their availability for purchase nor delivery terms has been confirmed. No town purchase has been authorized. My neighbour now says builder reported two hundred fresh loaves ready. That may be the same order, but I have not verified it or learned who the bread is intended for.

Several townsfolk have repeated the odd phrase 'bridge or port change at bakery,' sometimes naming baker and neighbour as present. I found no baker when I visited. My neighbour explicitly cannot substantiate any change: they heard Townsfolk thirteen mention it and recall no definite announcement. I should treat this as gossip rather than evidence of a real bridge or port project.

My neighbour also reports that innkeeper wants to speak to me about an unresolved account and a spoiled batch. I have asked that innkeeper be directed to my office. This could concern the bread trade, but I do not yet know. No council letters had arrived when I asked the secretary; I requested a further check and a report at half past four.

The lighting work, the large bread order, and the innkeeper's concerns may simply be separate practical matters. They could also relate to some gathering, but I have no direct evidence of that. I feel there is business circulating without reaching me clearly. My next steps are to keep my office appointment, hear the innkeeper and secretary, ask the baker directly about the bread and rumour, and attend the lighting inspection without turning speculation into fact.
